title: Whatever is born will pass
hook: jo upjio so binas hai: whatever is born will perish, today or tomorrow (Salok M9 52, ang 1429)

segments.voice: Yesterday: worry about the unexpected, and your line: nothing stays. Did a predictable worry come back, and did you set it down? Today, the next salok goes one step further. Day six hundred three.

A gardener plants tomatoes in May. By August the vines are taller than the fence and the kitchen counter is covered in fruit. By October the first frost comes, and in one night the whole bed goes black. The gardener knows this is coming. She plants anyway, every spring, and doesn't stand at the window in July grieving the frost. She picks, she cooks, she gives bags of tomatoes to the neighbors. The ending is written into the seed packet. Guru Tegh Bahadur's next salok says the same thing about everything that has ever been born, and then it says what to do with the summer. Today: whatever is born will pass.
screen: `TOMATOES IN MAY.` → `FROST IN OCTOBER.` → `THE ENDING IS IN THE SEED PACKET.`

segments.voice: Salok fifty-two, on Ang fourteen twenty-nine, begins: jo upjio so binas hai. Upjio is what has sprung up, been born, been made. Binas is what perishes, comes undone. Whatever sprang up will come undone. Then three short words: paro aaj kai kaal. It falls today, or tomorrow. Kaal here means tomorrow, and some readers hear a shadow in it, since the same sound also names time, and death. Notice the line doesn't say when. It doesn't threaten. It just refuses to pretend. Today or tomorrow: the only open question is the date. The second line is where the salok turns. In paraphrase: Nanak says, sing the praises of the Lord, and let go of all the janjaal. Janjaal is a lovely, tangled word: the snares, the nets, the knots of busyness and attachment we get caught in. Like a fishing net left in a shed for a year, knotted into itself. So the Guru puts two things side by side. Everything passes. Therefore, sing. Not therefore, despair; not therefore, nothing matters. The fact of passing is given as the reason to spend the time well. This is the same pattern the gardener lives by. The frost isn't a reason not to plant. It's the reason to pick the tomatoes now and give some away. In Sikh life, singing the praises means the Name, kirtan, the daily banis. And Sikhs have a word for the frost's place in it: hukam, the order of things. Accepting that the frost comes is not the same as not caring about the garden.
screen: `UPJIO, BINAS: SPRUNG UP, COME UNDONE.` · `TODAY OR TOMORROW: ONLY THE DATE IS OPEN.` · `JANJAAL: THE TANGLED NET.` · `IT PASSES, SO SING.` · then, large: `TODAY OR TOMORROW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with that calmly. Settle, and let your breath find its own pace. Think of one thing you love that is passing: a season of your kids' lives, a friendship as it is right now, your own body at this age. Don't push the thought away, and don't chase it into sadness. Just hold it, the way you'd hold a ripe tomato: gently, because it won't keep. Then think of one way to enjoy it today. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on the out-breath. The bell holds the time.
Whatever is born will pass. Jo upjio so binas hai: what sprang up comes undone, today or tomorrow, so sing while it's summer.
screen: `WHATEVER IS BORN WILL PASS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: today or tomorrow. Pick one thing that won't keep, a call, a meal, an hour with someone, and do it today, not tomorrow. Day six hundred three.

howItsDone: Sikhs hear salok fifty-two among Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks at the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib.

fork.reveal: Nanak says sing the Lord's praises and drop the janjaal. the passing is the reason to spend the summer well, not to stop planting.

original.note: Gurmukhi: janjaal, the snares and tangles of worldly busyness, from salok fifty-two.

trapdoor: what you thought: whatever is born will pass is a gloomy line.
what it means: it names the one sure fact, then says: so sing, and drop the tangles.
what a scholar hears: some readers hear time and death behind kaal, tomorrow; the salok pairs binas with janjaal, a common Gurbani word for the snare of attachment.

sources.ref: Salok Mahalla 9, salok 52 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429)
hukam: the divine order, accepted at a death

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): the claim that kaal also means time and death is now 'some readers hear', not a stated double meaning; hook no longer generalizes about every gardener; replaced the death-and-hukam ending, which anticipated day 609's bhog-after-a-death lesson.
Transliteration jo upjio so binas hai paro aaj kai kaal / naanak har gun gaai lai chhaad sagal janjaal: confirm wording and numbering as salok 52.
Claim that kaal can mean tomorrow, time and death: confirm the double sense is accepted for this line.
Gurmukhi spelling ਜੰਜਾਲ: confirm against the line as printed.
